title: Financial Statements & General-Purpose Reporting
description: Master the purpose, structure and relationships of the primary financial statements and general-purpose financial reporting.
html:
The purpose of financial reporting

General-purpose financial reporting provides financial information that is useful to existing and potential investors, lenders and other creditors when they make decisions about providing resources to an entity.

FAR requires more than memorizing the names of financial statements.

You need to understand what each statement reports, how the statements connect and how transactions flow through them.

CPA mindset

When a transaction occurs, ask:

  1. What accounts changed?
  2. Which financial statement is affected?
  3. Does the transaction affect income, equity, cash, or more than one statement?
  4. Is additional disclosure required?

The primary financial statements

Balance Sheet

Reports assets, liabilities and stockholders' equity at a specific date.

Assets = Liabilities + Equity

Income Statement

Reports revenues, expenses, gains and losses included in net income for a period of time.

Revenues and Gains − Expenses and Losses = Net Income

Statement of Comprehensive Income

Reports comprehensive income, which includes net income plus other comprehensive income.

Comprehensive Income = Net Income + OCI

Statement of Cash Flows

Explains changes in cash and cash equivalents through operating, investing and financing activities.

Statement of Changes in Equity

Explains changes in equity accounts during the reporting period.

Notes to Financial Statements

Provide information necessary to understand amounts, policies, uncertainties and other matters presented in the financial statements.

Point in time vs period of time

This distinction is very important.

Point in Time

Balance Sheet

Example: December 31, 20X6

Period of Time

Income Statement

Comprehensive Income

Cash Flows

Changes in Equity

CPA trap

The balance sheet reports a financial position at a particular date.

Statements such as the income statement report activity occurring during a period.

How the statements connect

The statements are not independent documents. Information flows between them.

Example

Assume a corporation earns $100,000 of net income and declares $30,000 of dividends during the year.

Increase in Retained Earnings = Net Income − Dividends
$100,000 − $30,000 = $70,000 increase

The $100,000 net income comes from the income statement.

That income affects retained earnings, which is an equity account reported on the balance sheet.

Dividends reduce retained earnings but are not expenses on the income statement.

Important CPA distinction

Dividends ≠ Expense

Dividends are distributions to owners and generally reduce retained earnings.

Accrual accounting matters

Financial statements prepared under accrual accounting do not simply report cash receipts and cash payments.

Example

A company performs $40,000 of services in December and collects the cash in January.

Assuming the applicable revenue recognition requirements have been satisfied in December, December financial reporting recognizes:

Account
Debit
Credit
Accounts Receivable
$40,000
—
Revenue
—
$40,000

The income statement therefore reports the revenue in December even though December cash did not increase.

The balance sheet reports the related Accounts Receivable.

Financial statement articulation

The financial statements should tell a connected financial story.

  • Net income affects retained earnings.
  • OCI affects accumulated other comprehensive income within equity.
  • Ending cash on the statement of cash flows should reconcile to the cash reported on the balance sheet.
  • Equity transactions flow through the statement of changes in equity and ending balance-sheet equity.

Notes are part of financial reporting

A number on the face of a financial statement may not provide enough information by itself.

Notes can explain accounting policies, significant estimates, debt terms, contingencies, commitments and other relevant information.

FAR questions may therefore require you to determine not only the correct amount, but also how an item should be presented or disclosed.

Worked CPA-style example

Assume the following during the year:

Beginning Retained Earnings $250,000
Net Income $90,000
Dividends ($20,000)

Step 1 — Begin with retained earnings

$250,000

Step 2 — Add net income

$250,000 + $90,000 = $340,000

Step 3 — Subtract dividends

$340,000 − $20,000 = $320,000

Ending retained earnings is $320,000.

Why this matters

This question connects the income statement to equity and ultimately to the balance sheet.

FAR frequently tests relationships between accounts and statements rather than isolated definitions.

What you should know after this lesson

  • Know what each primary financial statement reports.
  • Distinguish point-in-time reporting from period reporting.
  • Understand that accrual income and cash flow are different measures.
  • Understand how net income, retained earnings and equity connect.
  • Understand that dividends are not income-statement expenses.
  • Understand the role of financial statement notes and disclosures.
  • Think about presentation and disclosure in addition to calculation.

quiz.prompt: A corporation begins the year with $400,000 of retained earnings, reports $120,000 of net income and declares $35,000 of dividends. What is ending retained earnings?
quiz.explanation: Ending retained earnings equals beginning retained earnings plus net income minus dividends: $400,000 + $120,000 − $35,000 = $485,000.
